# Cardiac Amyloidosis: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Cardiac amyloidosis is an infiltrative disorder in which misfolded protein deposits as insoluble amyloid fibrils within the myocardial extracellular space, producing a progressively restrictive cardiomyopathy. The amyloidoses are a group of protein-folding disorders in which one or more organs are infiltrated by deposits known as amyloid; the prognosis is determined both by the organ(s) involved and the type of amyloid, and amyloid involvement of the heart carries the worst prognosis of any involved organ. The two principal types affecting the heart are immunoglobulin light-chain (AL) amyloidosis and transthyretin (ATTR) amyloidosis. Once considered rare and untreatable, cardiac amyloidosis has been transformed by advances in non-invasive imaging and the arrival of effective disease-modifying therapy. Transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis is an increasingly recognized cause of heart failure and mortality worldwide, and advances in non-invasive diagnosis coupled with effective treatments have shifted it from a rare and untreatable disease to a relatively prevalent condition that clinicians should consider on a daily basis.

## Pathophysiology and epidemiology

In ATTR amyloidosis, transthyretin is a protein synthesized primarily in the liver that transports vitamin A and thyroxine, normally circulating as a tetramer; through gene mutation or aging, TTR can become unstable and break into oligomers that aggregate into insoluble fibrils that deposit in tissues. Two forms exist: amyloid fibril formation results from age-related failure of homoeostatic mechanisms in wild-type ATTR (non-hereditary) or from destabilizing mutations in variant ATTR (hereditary form). The Val122Ile variant is an age-dependent autosomal dominant cardiomyopathy too common to be overlooked as a cause of significant heart disease in elderly African Americans. The disease is more common than previously appreciated: recent studies suggest that up to 10–15% of older adults with heart failure may harbor unrecognized wild-type ATTR. In AL amyloidosis, a clonal plasma cell population produces amyloidogenic light chains; AL amyloidosis is a rare, often fatal disease in which cardiomyopathy is a common presenting feature, and cardiac amyloid infiltration is the leading predictor of death.

## Clinical presentation and diagnosis

ATTR-CM has historically eluded recognition. It has been historically difficult to diagnose due to diverse clinical manifestations and nonspecific, variable electrocardiogram and echocardiogram findings. Extracardiac clues are valuable: associated features, including carpal tunnel syndrome and lumbar spinal stenosis, raise suspicion and may afford a means for early diagnosis.

The most important diagnostic advance has been bone scintigraphy. Cardiac transthyretin amyloidosis was historically diagnosed by biopsy, but it has long been recognized that technetium-labeled bone scintigraphy tracers can localize to myocardial amyloid deposits, and use of this imaging modality has been revisited. In a landmark multicenter study, myocardial radiotracer uptake on bone scintigraphy was over 99% sensitive and 86% specific for cardiac ATTR amyloid, with false positives almost exclusively attributable to light-chain disease. Consequently, the diagnosis can be made with non-invasive nuclear imaging when there is no evidence of a monoclonal protein. Contemporary algorithms emphasize this principle: with reasonable clinical suspicion, providers should first rule out AL amyloidosis via monoclonal protein screening; if negative, nuclear bone scintigraphy and genetic testing are completed to categorize patients as hereditary or wild-type.

## Prognosis and staging

Untreated ATTR-CM is progressive. The median survival from diagnosis in untreated patients is consistently around 3.5 years, but is dependent on the stage of disease. In a large series, median overall survival from diagnosis of wild-type ATTR was 3.6 years and did not change over time. Biomarker-based staging systems guide prognosis using troponin and natriuretic peptides, including a widely validated system that established and validated a prognostic staging system applicable to patients with both wild-type and hereditary ATTR. In AL amyloidosis, prognosis is dominated by cardiac involvement; median survival from diagnosis for patients with AL amyloidosis and cardiomyopathy ranges from 4 months to 2 years.

## Disease-modifying therapy

The therapeutic landscape has expanded rapidly. The proof-of-concept for TTR stabilization came from neuropathy trials, in which tafamidis was evaluated over 18 months in patients with early-stage V30M transthyretin familial amyloid polyneuropathy in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled design. In the pivotal cardiac trial, tafamidis binds to transthyretin, preventing tetramer dissociation and amyloidogenesis, and 441 patients were randomized to tafamidis or placebo for 30 months. Tafamidis was associated with reductions in all-cause mortality and cardiovascular-related hospitalizations and reduced the decline in functional capacity and quality of life compared with placebo.

A second stabilizer followed: acoramidis is a high-affinity TTR stabilizer that inhibits dissociation of tetrameric TTR and leads to more than 90% stabilization across the dosing interval as measured ex vivo. Gene-silencing approaches reduce hepatic TTR production. In ATTR-CM, patisiran over 12 months resulted in preserved functional capacity in patients with ATTR cardiac amyloidosis. This built upon the earlier polyneuropathy trial in which patisiran improved multiple clinical manifestations of hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis. Most recently, vutrisiran demonstrated mortality benefit: among patients with ATTR-CM, treatment with vutrisiran led to a lower risk of death from any cause and cardiovascular events than placebo and preserved functional capacity and quality of life. A comparative synthesis notes that patisiran preserved functional capacity but did not reduce mortality at 12 months, acoramidis was superior to placebo on a hierarchical endpoint, and vutrisiran significantly improved a composite of death and cardiovascular events.

For AL amyloidosis, treatment targets the plasma cell clone, and prognosis depends on the extent of cardiac involvement, with cardiac biomarkers guiding the choice of therapy. Late diagnosis results in approximately 30% of patients presenting with advanced, irreversible organ involvement and dying within a few months despite modern treatments.

## Conclusion

Cardiac amyloidosis has evolved into a recognizable and treatable disease. Authoritative guidance underscores this paradigm shift: enthusiasm has grown from three simultaneous advances—imaging techniques that allow accurate noninvasive diagnosis without biopsy, observational studies indicating underrecognition among heart failure patients, and approved therapies based on elucidation of amyloid formation. Because therapy for ATTR-CM may be most effective when administered before significant cardiac dysfunction, early identification of affected individuals with readily available noninvasive tests is essential. A high index of suspicion, judicious use of bone scintigraphy with exclusion of monoclonal protein, and timely initiation of disease-modifying therapy now offer meaningful improvements in survival and quality of life.
